description_intro: Eight recent jailbreak tweaks covering AI keyboard actions, Home Screen controls, music, AirPods compatibility, lyrics and the Phone app. Every feature image comes from a package, developer or clearly credited editorial source. This is a source-checked comparison, not a hands-on compatibility test. Verify your exact iOS version, jailbreak, bootstrap, architecture, dependencies and current package details before installing.

scenes.title: 8 fresh jailbreak tweaks with real screenshots
scenes.subtitle: AI, Home Screen, music, AirPods, lyrics and calls

visual.credit: Authentic package screenshots · all sources credited below

scenes.narration: A jailbreak can change almost every part of an iPhone, but a useful tweak video should show what each package really looks like, not a row of invented icons. In this source-checked guide, we are looking at eight very different packages: an AI keyboard assistant, a Home Screen control menu, upcoming-song controls, AirPods compatibility, advanced keyboard gestures, two Lock Screen music upgrades, and a complete Phone app toolkit. Every feature image comes from the official package or developer listing, except PodsGrant, where the real preference screenshots are clearly credited to an established editorial source and the release warning comes directly from the developer. This is not a hands-on compatibility test. Before installing anything, compare the current source page with your exact iOS version, jailbreak, bootstrap, architecture and dependencies. Narration uses an AI-generated voice, while the research, script, design and editorial choices are original Next Jailbreak work.

scenes.short_title: HelloKeyboardAI Adds AI Gestures to the iPhone Keyboard #Shorts
scenes.title: HelloKeyboardAI
scenes.subtitle: Trigger AI text actions without leaving the keyboard
scenes.narration: First is HelloKeyboardAI, a paid keyboard tweak built around quick AI activation. Its preference pane lets users assign actions to upward, downward, left and right keyboard gestures. The published feature overview also describes analyzing existing or selected text, replacing it with a response, or copying the analyzed result to the clipboard. Other configurable entry points involve keyboard controls such as the bottom bar, dictation button, dock or globe key. Havoc currently lists support from iOS 14.0 through 17.3.1 and identifies rootless compatibility, with a listed price of five dollars and ninety-nine cents. One detail needs attention: Next Jailbreak recorded a 6.3.0-6 package-feed build while the public product page displayed 6.3.0-3 when checked. Confirm the exact build offered by your package manager. This is the tweak to compare if you want AI commands integrated into typing instead of repeatedly switching to another application.

scenes.short_title: IconTweak2 Opens a Control Menu from Home Screen Icons #Shorts
scenes.title: IconTweak2
scenes.subtitle: Swipe an app icon to open its control menu
scenes.narration: IconTweak2 has a simple core idea: swipe an app icon to reveal a control menu. The real screenshots show a native-looking action sheet appearing directly over the Home Screen, plus the preference interface used to configure the behavior. That is much clearer than describing it as a generic icon utility. Its value is speed. App-related controls stay beside the icon that they affect, instead of being buried across several settings pages. Havoc lists iOS 15.0 through 26.0.1, marks the package as rootless-compatible and shows a price of two dollars and ninety-nine cents. There is also a version difference to verify. The package feed recorded 1.0.2, while the public Havoc page displayed 1.0.1 when checked. Use the version offered by the official source and inspect the action list on your installed build. If you already use another icon-gesture tweak, test for gesture conflicts before enabling both.

scenes.short_title: NextUp 3 Lets You Skip the Next Song Before It Starts #Shorts
scenes.title: NextUp 3
scenes.subtitle: See and skip the next song from Now Playing
scenes.narration: NextUp 3 adds information that Apple normally keeps inside the playback queue. It shows the upcoming song from supported Now Playing surfaces and lets you skip that track before it begins. The current package information covers the Lock Screen and Control Center, with official screenshots showing how the extra track information fits beside the normal media controls. The listing includes Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube Music among the supported integrations. Havoc currently presents NextUp 3 as free, rootless-compatible and available for iOS 14.2 through 26.0.1. App support matters as much as iOS support here, so confirm that your exact player is listed before installing. Also remember that older public NextUp documentation contains historical integrations that may not describe the current version. If you frequently skip songs after only a few seconds, seeing the next item early can make the playback queue much easier to manage.

scenes.short_title: PodsGrant Warning: iOS 17 Needs a Different Build #Shorts
scenes.title: PodsGrant 0.5.4
scenes.subtitle: Newer AirPods support—with an important iOS 17 warning

visual.credit: Real screenshots · Tools 4 Hack; release notes · LNSSPsd

scenes.narration: PodsGrant is a compatibility tweak for pairing newer AirPods or selected Beats hardware with an older jailbroken device. The real preference images show model choices, product identification controls and options for applying the configuration. This package needs more caution than the others because the developer's 0.5.4 release note contains two explicit warnings. First, version 0.5.4 does not work on iOS 17. The developer directs iOS 17 users to 0.5.5 prerelease 3. Second, the original arm package uploaded for the rootful branch did not work on the developer's machine, so a rebuilt arm asset was added from the same codebase. Rootless arm64 has its own asset. Do not select a file only by version number. Match the iOS version and architecture, then read the full release note. PodsGrant can solve a very specific hardware compatibility problem, but using the wrong build is more likely to create confusion than fix it.

scenes.short_title: SwipeExtenderX Adds 27 Actions to iPhone Keyboard Keys #Shorts
scenes.title: SwipeExtenderX
scenes.subtitle: Assign swipe and long-press commands to keys
scenes.narration: SwipeExtenderX turns ordinary keyboard keys into gesture shortcuts. Chariz lists twenty-seven actions that can be assigned through swipes or long presses. The options include common editing commands such as select, cut, copy, paste, undo, redo and delete, along with cursor movement, keyboard dismissal, dictation and menu actions. The official screenshots also show per-key configuration, custom labels and keyboard color controls. Chariz currently lists iOS 14 and later, support for iPhone, iPad and iPod touch, and rootless compatibility. It also states that third-party keyboard applications are not supported, so this is intended for Apple's keyboard. The automated article originally covered feed version 1.6.1, but Chariz displayed 1.6.2 when checked. Install the current official build rather than searching for the older one. Start with only one or two gestures, because a keyboard full of unfamiliar swipes can slow typing before it improves it.

scenes.short_title: Reo Replaces the iPhone Lock Screen Music Player #Shorts
scenes.title: Reo 4.0.1
scenes.subtitle: A custom artwork-led Now Playing layout
scenes.narration: Reo is a visual replacement for the stock Lock Screen music player. Instead of changing the whole system, it focuses on the hierarchy of album artwork, track information and playback controls. The official images show the finished player layouts and the preferences used to configure them, which is essential for a tweak whose main purpose is visual presentation. Havoc lists version 4.0.1 at one dollar and ninety-nine cents, with support from iOS 14.0 through 17.3.1 and a rootless-compatible package. Reo is best compared against other Now Playing replacements, not against a complete theme. Those packages often modify the same Lock Screen area, so overlapping artwork or controls can come from a conflict rather than Reo itself. If you install it, test the default layout with other media tweaks temporarily disabled, then change one option at a time. Choose Reo when album art and a redesigned player are the main goal.

scenes.short_title: LSLyrics Puts Time-Synced Lyrics on the Lock Screen #Shorts
scenes.title: LSLyrics 2.0
scenes.subtitle: Follow time-synced lyrics without opening the music app
scenes.narration: LSLyrics places time-synced song lyrics directly on the Lock Screen. As playback moves forward, the active line changes without requiring the music app to stay open. The official screenshots show the normal lyric presentation, an immersive full-screen mode and the preference interface. In full-screen mode, normal Lock Screen elements can be hidden so the lyrics and artwork take priority. Havoc lists version 2.0 at one dollar and forty-nine cents, with support from iOS 14.0 through 17.7.11, both iPhone and iPad, and rootless compatibility. Lyrics still depend on supported playback information and availability for the current song; a compatibility range cannot guarantee that every track has synchronized data. Another Lock Screen tweak can also compete for the same space. LSLyrics is the better choice than Reo when the words are the focus. Reo is primarily a player redesign, while LSLyrics is specifically about following the song.

scenes.short_title: Phonehub Adds Caller ID and Auto Redial to iPhone #Shorts
scenes.title: Phonehub 1.1.3
scenes.subtitle: Caller ID, auto redial, dual SIM and smarter call controls
scenes.narration: Phonehub is the broadest system utility in this list. It expands several stages of the Phone app rather than adding one isolated button. The developer lists caller identification through multiple global and regional lookup sources, with the option to switch the lookup engine during a call. Other features include a SIM picker before dialing on dual-SIM devices, automatic redial for busy, unanswered or unavailable calls, proximity-aware loudspeaker behavior that respects Bluetooth and CarPlay, call-connect vibration, country-code normalization and local caching. Havoc lists version 1.1.3 at three dollars and ninety-nine cents for iOS 15.0 through 17.0, with rootless support. Caller identification deserves a privacy check because number information may be compared through the selected service, and provider availability can vary by region. Configure one feature group at a time, then place a non-urgent test call. Phonehub is the package to investigate if the stock Phone app feels too limited.

scenes.title: Which of these eight should you compare first?
scenes.subtitle: Start with the problem—not the most dramatic screenshot
facts: System utilities: IconTweak2, PodsGrant or Phonehub

visual.credit: Authentic source screenshots · sources listed in description

scenes.narration: These eight packages do not compete in one simple ranking, so choose by the problem you want to solve. For writing and text workflows, compare HelloKeyboardAI with SwipeExtenderX. One focuses on AI text actions, while the other focuses on local editing, clipboard and cursor gestures. For music, NextUp 3 is the functional queue tool, Reo is the player redesign, and LSLyrics is the synchronized-words experience. IconTweak2 belongs to the Home Screen because it keeps app controls beside their icons. PodsGrant is only relevant when newer headphones and older software need a compatibility bridge, and its release warning must be followed exactly. Phonehub is for users who want a wider Phone app upgrade and are comfortable reviewing the privacy terms of caller-ID services. None of these is automatically the best for every device. The useful first choice is the tweak whose feature matches your daily frustration and whose current source explicitly supports your setup.

scenes.title: Five checks that prevent most bad installs
scenes.subtitle: Version, iOS, architecture, conflicts and recovery
facts: Check rootful, rootless or RootHide build
Keep a safe way to disable the package

visual.credit: Real settings screenshots · sources credited in description

scenes.narration: Before installing any package from this video, complete five checks. First, open the original source and verify the current version. The feed and public page sometimes display different builds, as we saw with HelloKeyboardAI and IconTweak2. Second, confirm the iOS range instead of guessing from an architecture label. Third, match the package to your bootstrap: rootful, rootless, RootHide or another environment are not interchangeable words. Fourth, identify conflicts. Keyboard tweaks, Lock Screen players and icon gestures often modify the same process as another package. Test one change at a time. Fifth, keep a recovery path so you can disable or remove a package if SpringBoard or an application behaves unexpectedly. The full written guides and every source link are available at NextSolution dot c c. Tell us which tweak you want to see in a full hands-on guide. Narration in this video uses an AI-generated voice. Thanks for watching Next Jailbreak.
